items.prompt: An API fleet is scaled out and instances are routinely replaced. Which implementation lets any healthy instance serve any request?
constraints: Instances do not share local memory.
The client may be routed to a different instance on every request.
Durable business state is stored outside the process.

options.text: Keep request processing deterministic and store session or business state in a shared managed store or verifiable client token, not in instance memory.
Store all state in local process memory and require the load balancer to find the same instance forever.
Write business state to the instance's temporary disk because replacement preserves the disk automatically.
Disable health checks so requests continue reaching instances that hold older state.

feedback.Reason: Stateless compute is replaceable because durable state is externalized and each instance can process a request independently.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The application tier can scale horizontally when requests do not depend on one process's memory or local filesystem.
Details.scenarioApplication: Any healthy instance validates the request, reads required state from the selected store, and writes changes through the owning service.
Details.errorCorrection: Affinity and local state reduce elasticity, temporary disks are not durable instance-independent storage, and disabled health checks route to unhealthy capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: External state adds latency and a dependency, so the store's availability, consistency, and capacity must be designed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Local memory is lost or unavailable when a different instance handles the request.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Instance-local temporary storage does not provide durable shared state across replacement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Health checks are needed to remove failed targets rather than route traffic to them.

items.prompt: Users must keep a shopping cart while application instances scale and fail independently. Which state location is appropriate?
constraints: The cart must survive an instance replacement.
The application tier is horizontally scaled.
Cart loss is a customer-visible failure.

options.text: Store the cart in a shared durable or managed session store with an explicit expiration and consistency policy, while keeping instances replaceable.
Store the cart only in each instance's memory and use sticky sessions as the durability mechanism.
Store the cart in a load balancer health-check response because health checks are shared across instances.
Store the cart in an application log and reconstruct it from log order on every request.

feedback.Reason: A cart is user state and needs a shared state contract when compute instances are disposable.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A shared store makes the state available to any healthy instance and allows TTL, access, and capacity behavior to be controlled explicitly.
Details.scenarioApplication: The API reads and updates the cart through the store, and expired or unavailable state has an explicit product outcome.
Details.errorCorrection: Sticky sessions are routing behavior rather than durability, health checks do not store carts, and logs are not a transactional cart database.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A shared store adds dependency and cost; token-based state may reduce reads but has size, security, and revocation constraints.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Session affinity does not protect local memory from instance failure or replacement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Health-check responses are not a state store and are not scoped to users.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Logs are append-oriented evidence and are not a safe read-write cart model.

items.prompt: A low-risk session contains only a user identifier, expiry, and authorization claims, and the API must avoid a session-store read on every request. Which approach is a candidate?
constraints: The token must be integrity-protected.
Claims must have an explicit expiry and scope.
Revocation and sensitive data requirements must be addressed.

options.text: Use a signed or encrypted token with minimal claims and short lifetime, and validate signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and authorization on every request.
Use an unsigned token containing the user's permissions because clients cannot alter browser data.
Put the user's password in the token so the API can avoid an identity lookup.
Use a token with no expiry because stateless sessions cannot be revoked otherwise.

feedback.Reason: Stateless tokens can reduce session-store reads only when their integrity, lifetime, claims, and revocation boundaries are explicit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The API verifies token cryptography and registered claims before using the token as an authorization input.
Details.scenarioApplication: The token contains no secret or excessive data, expires quickly, and the system has a strategy for user disablement or permission change.
Details.errorCorrection: Unsigned claims are tamperable, passwords must never be placed in tokens, and no-expiry tokens enlarge compromise and revocation risk.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tokens improve availability of the session path but make claim staleness, size, and revocation design more important.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unsigned client-controlled claims cannot be trusted for authorization.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Embedding passwords creates a severe credential disclosure risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An unlimited lifetime increases the impact of token theft and makes policy changes difficult.

items.prompt: An application currently uses load-balancer stickiness because sessions are local, but one instance is overloaded and replacement logs users out. What is the better long-term direction?
constraints: Traffic should distribute across healthy capacity.
Instance replacement must not lose sessions.
The session contract can be changed.

options.text: Externalize session state or use carefully governed tokens, then remove the dependency on stickiness so the tier can balance and replace instances freely.
Increase stickiness duration indefinitely so the overloaded instance receives all returning users.
Disable health checks while retaining local sessions so failed instances remain available to their users.
Copy local session memory to a random instance only when the load balancer returns an error.

feedback.Reason: Stickiness can mask local-state coupling but does not provide balanced capacity or resilience during replacement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: External state lets the load balancer select any healthy target and keeps state independent of target lifecycle.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team migrates sessions, tests expiration and concurrent updates, and removes affinity after all requests can use the shared contract.
Details.errorCorrection: Longer affinity worsens imbalance, disabled health checks route to failed targets, and reactive memory copying is incomplete and unsafe.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A migration may require dual-read or session invalidation decisions, but the final design should have one canonical state path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Longer stickiness reinforces imbalance and does not survive instance failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Disabling health checks sends traffic to unhealthy targets.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Ad hoc copying cannot guarantee consistency, completeness, or secure state transfer.

items.prompt: Users upload large files while API instances are autoscaled. Which pattern keeps file transfer from consuming application instance capacity?
constraints: Files must be durable.
The API should authorize uploads.
The application should receive metadata or completion events rather than proxy every byte.

options.text: Issue a scoped, time-limited upload URL for Amazon S3 and let the application process metadata or an object-created event after the upload.
Store every file in application instance memory until a user downloads it.
Put the file in a session cookie so any web instance can retrieve it without a storage service.
Send the file through the database connection pool and keep the transaction open until processing completes.

feedback.Reason: Direct object-storage upload externalizes large transfer state and keeps the application tier focused on authorization and workflow.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A presigned URL grants bounded access to an object operation; the API retains ownership of metadata and downstream processing decisions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The client uploads to a controlled key, the application validates size and content, and an event or status record starts processing.
Details.errorCorrection: Instance memory is not durable, cookies are small client-side state and expose data, and long database transactions consume scarce connections.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Direct upload requires careful key, content, expiration, encryption, and event validation design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Instance memory is limited and disappears with replacement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Cookies are not appropriate for large durable files and can expose content to the client.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Long file transfers through database transactions create contention and failure coupling.

items.prompt: A client retries a purchase request after a timeout and the first request may have succeeded. Which application design prevents two charges?
constraints: Network failure makes the result ambiguous.
The operation has a business identifier.
A retry must return the original outcome when possible.

options.text: Require an idempotency key, persist the key and outcome with the state transition, and return the same result for a duplicate request.
Disable retries and assume a timeout means the purchase never occurred.
Generate a new charge identifier for every retry so the database cannot detect duplicates.
Store the key only in the application instance memory that receives the first request.

feedback.Reason: Idempotency makes retry behavior safe when the caller cannot know whether the first state transition completed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A durable idempotency record binds a client operation key to the committed result and is checked atomically with the business operation.
Details.scenarioApplication: A retry receives the original success or a defined in-progress/conflict outcome instead of creating a second charge.
Details.errorCorrection: Disabling retries harms availability, new keys defeat duplicate detection, and local memory disappears or is not shared.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The idempotency record needs retention, cleanup, concurrency, and failure semantics aligned to the business operation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A timeout is ambiguous and disabling retries does not establish the actual business state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: New identifiers make each retry look like a new operation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Instance-local keys cannot protect retries routed to another instance.

items.prompt: A session store grows without bound because users never explicitly sign out. Which control is required?
constraints: Inactive sessions do not need indefinite retention.
Security requires bounded credential lifetime.
The application must handle an expired session clearly.

options.text: Set an explicit TTL and renewal policy for session records, and return an authenticated-expired outcome that requires reauthentication.
Retain every session forever because more history always improves availability.
Delete sessions randomly whenever storage is full without notifying clients.
Extend every session on every request with no maximum lifetime or idle limit.

feedback.Reason: Session state needs retention and security bounds; TTL prevents unbounded growth and limits stale credentials.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A TTL removes inactive or expired state according to a documented lifecycle, while renewal rules define how active sessions continue.
Details.scenarioApplication: The API treats a missing or expired record as a sign-in requirement rather than silently creating a new identity.
Details.errorCorrection: Infinite retention grows cost and risk, random eviction creates confusing behavior, and unbounded renewal defeats session lifetime controls.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Short TTLs improve security but can increase reauthentication; the choice should match user experience and threat model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Indefinite retention wastes capacity and keeps stale session credentials available.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unannounced random deletion creates an uncontrolled product state and can cause data loss.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Idle and absolute lifetime limits are important even when sessions are active.

items.prompt: An administrator disables a user and the user's token remains valid for hours. Which state strategy best supports rapid revocation?
constraints: Disablement must take effect quickly.
The application currently uses token-based authentication.
The design should not expose sensitive credentials.

options.text: Use short-lived access tokens with a revocation or session-state check appropriate to the threat model, and make refresh or disablement controlled by the identity boundary.
Use tokens with a permanent lifetime because stateless tokens cannot be invalidated.
Put the disablement flag only in one application instance's memory.
Ask clients to delete the token and assume a malicious or offline client will comply.

feedback.Reason: Token convenience must be balanced with a revocation design; short lifetimes and controlled session state limit the disablement window.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The identity system and application can combine short access-token lifetimes, refresh-token controls, deny lists, or session checks according to required revocation speed.
Details.scenarioApplication: A disabled user cannot refresh or renew access, and the application enforces the selected check on protected operations.
Details.errorCorrection: Permanent tokens make compromise durable, local flags are not shared, and client deletion is not an enforcement control.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More frequent checks or shorter lifetimes add latency or user friction, so revocation objectives must be explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Permanent access increases the impact of a stolen or disabled credential.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: One instance's flag cannot protect requests routed to other instances.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security enforcement cannot depend on an untrusted client deleting its own token.

items.prompt: Session reads are frequent and the authoritative session store is healthy but adds latency. Which pattern can reduce repeated reads without making cache the source of truth?
constraints: The session store remains authoritative.
Cache misses and eviction are expected.
Expired or revoked sessions must not remain usable beyond policy.

options.text: Use a cache-aside session cache with bounded TTL, invalidation or version checks, and a miss path to the authoritative store.
Write sessions only to the cache and treat eviction as a user logout with no authoritative record.
Cache every session forever so revocation never requires a store read.
Return any cached session for the user ID without checking its tenant, version, or expiry.

feedback.Reason: Cache-aside accelerates reads while preserving an authoritative state store and explicit freshness and revocation behavior.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The application reads the cache first, loads a miss from the source, and updates or invalidates entries when authoritative state changes.
Details.scenarioApplication: A cache miss does not lose a session, and a revoked or expired record cannot be resurrected by a stale entry.
Details.errorCorrection: Cache-only sessions are lost on eviction, infinite caching defeats revocation, and unscoped entries can leak state across users or tenants.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Caching adds consistency and invalidation complexity, so it is valuable only when latency or load reduction justifies it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Eviction would destroy the only state and makes availability depend on cache retention.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Infinite TTL prevents timely expiry and revocation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A cache key must preserve identity, tenant, version, and expiry boundaries.

items.prompt: A user can open the same account from two devices and update preferences concurrently. What must the session or profile state model define?
constraints: Writes can race.
The state has an owner.
The product must define how conflicting updates are handled.

options.text: Define ownership, version or conditional-write behavior, and conflict semantics rather than assuming a shared session store makes concurrent writes safe.
Allow last-writer-wins without checking whether the overwritten value is still valid for the business operation.
Store one copy per device and call the values consistent because every device has a session.
Use cache eviction order as the conflict-resolution algorithm.

feedback.Reason: Externalizing state solves availability of reads but does not automatically solve concurrent business updates.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Conditional writes, versions, transactions, or domain-specific merge rules prevent a stale client from silently overwriting a newer state.
Details.scenarioApplication: The profile service rejects or resolves a conflicting update according to an explicit contract and returns a result the client can understand.
Details.errorCorrection: Unqualified last-writer-wins can lose business changes, per-device copies diverge, and eviction order has no correctness meaning.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Conflict protection can add retries or user resolution, but silent data loss is a worse failure mode.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Last-writer-wins without a condition can overwrite a valid concurrent change.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Copies per device create divergent authority unless synchronization and conflict rules exist.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cache lifecycle events do not represent business ordering or correctness.

items.prompt: Which test best validates that an application tier is truly stateless?
constraints: The application is behind a load balancer.
Instances can be replaced by automation.
Users must not lose durable state during replacement.

options.text: Terminate or drain the instance serving a session, route the next request to another healthy instance, and verify the session and business state remain correct.
Restart only the load balancer and verify its DNS name remains unchanged.
Increase the instance size and verify CPU utilization falls during a quiet period.
Disable the deployment controller so no instance can ever be replaced.

feedback.Reason: A replacement test exercises the actual assumption that state is external and any healthy instance can continue the request path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Failure or replacement removes local memory and files, exposing hidden affinity or local-state dependencies.
Details.scenarioApplication: The test checks authentication, session, idempotency, uploads, and in-flight behavior rather than only checking that DNS still resolves.
Details.errorCorrection: A load balancer restart, vertical scaling, or disabling replacement does not test instance independence.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Chaos or replacement testing needs safe environments and recovery controls, but it turns an architectural claim into evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Load balancer DNS continuity does not prove application state survives target replacement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Vertical capacity says nothing about local-state dependence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Preventing replacement hides the behavior the architecture must support.

items.prompt: Only the application tier should read session records, and administrators need a separate audit path. Which access model is best?
constraints: Session records contain sensitive data.
The runtime must use least privilege.
Administrative access must be traceable and separate.

options.text: Give the application runtime a narrowly scoped role for session operations and use a separate audited administrative role for support or investigation.
Use one administrator credential in every application instance so operations are simple.
Make the session store public and rely on random session identifiers for confidentiality.
Give every client direct session-store credentials so the application has no authorization responsibility.

feedback.Reason: Separate runtime and administrative identities preserve least privilege and make sensitive session access auditable.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM roles and resource policies can restrict actions and resource scope while CloudTrail or service logs record administrative access.
Details.scenarioApplication: The runtime can read or update only the records and operations it owns; support access requires a controlled role assumption.
Details.errorCorrection: Shared admin secrets, public stores, and client credentials expand authority and destroy the service boundary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fine-grained access requires policy maintenance and testing, but session data is an authentication and privacy boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A shared administrator credential gives every instance excessive authority and weakens attribution.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Random identifiers are not sufficient protection for a public data store.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Clients should not bypass the application authorization and data-model boundary.

items.prompt: A legacy application stores sessions in local files and must migrate to a scaled fleet without forcing all users to sign in again. What is the safest sequence?
constraints: The legacy and new paths may run concurrently.
Session data has a defined schema.
The final state must have one canonical store.

options.text: Introduce a shared session contract and store, migrate or dual-read existing sessions with clear precedence, validate behavior, then remove local-file dependence.
Delete all local sessions and deploy the new fleet because migration is not part of architecture.
Keep local files in both fleets forever and use a random instance to select the source of truth.
Copy files opportunistically after each request without versioning or conflict rules.

feedback.Reason: A staged migration makes the state contract explicit and ends with one canonical path instead of preserving competing stores.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Compatibility reads or migration tooling can bridge the old state while new requests converge on the shared store.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team measures migration completeness, resolves precedence, tests expiration and revocation, and removes the old path after evidence supports cutover.
Details.errorCorrection: Deleting state harms users, permanent competing stores create ambiguity, and opportunistic copies can lose or overwrite changes.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Migration adds temporary operational work, but it should converge to one canonical session owner rather than become a second architecture.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Deleting sessions is a data-loss shortcut, not a safe migration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Two unqualified stores make reads and writes ambiguous and prevent reliable revocation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Without versions and ownership, opportunistic copying cannot guarantee correctness.

items.prompt: A session contains only a small, non-sensitive preference and the service wants to avoid a server-side session store. What must be true before moving it to the client?
constraints: The client is untrusted.
The preference is not an authorization fact.
The application must validate and bound the value.

options.text: Treat the client value as an input, protect integrity if tamper detection is needed, validate it server-side, and never use it as proof of identity or privilege.
Trust any client preference as an authorization claim because it reduces server state.
Put credentials and internal database identifiers in the client value so the server can remain stateless.
Accept arbitrary unbounded client state because statelessness removes input-validation requirements.

feedback.Reason: Moving state to a client does not move trust to the client; the server must still validate and protect security decisions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Signed or encrypted representations can detect alteration, but authorization and business invariants remain server responsibilities.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service accepts a bounded preference and ignores or rejects invalid values without treating the preference as an entitlement.
Details.errorCorrection: Unsigned authorization claims, credentials, internal identifiers, and unbounded input create tampering, disclosure, and resource risks.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Client state reduces server storage but increases token size, key management, privacy, and revocation considerations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Client-controlled values cannot be trusted as authorization evidence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Credentials and internal identifiers should not be exposed to clients for convenience.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Stateless services still require strict input validation and size limits.

items.prompt: A long-running worker can be interrupted and restarted on another host. Which state pattern reduces duplicate or lost processing?
constraints: Work can be divided into retryable units.
The worker may fail after partial progress.
The output must be correct if a unit is retried.

options.text: Persist a durable work state or checkpoint, make each unit idempotent, and use an explicit lease, retry, and completion policy.
Keep progress only in worker memory and acknowledge the job before writing its output.
Disable retries because a second worker could process a unit twice.
Use the worker hostname as the durable checkpoint identifier because hosts are never replaced.

feedback.Reason: Durable progress and idempotent units let replacement workers resume or safely repeat work.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A lease or visibility boundary coordinates ownership while durable checkpoints and idempotent outputs protect against crashes and retries.
Details.scenarioApplication: A restarted worker can claim unfinished work, and a duplicate completion does not create an incorrect second output.
Details.errorCorrection: Memory is lost, early acknowledgment can lose output, disabling retries sacrifices recovery, and hostnames are not durable identities.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Checkpoint granularity and coordination add storage and complexity, but they define recovery behavior for long work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Local progress and early acknowledgment can lose work on failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Retries are needed for recoverable failures; correctness comes from idempotency and ownership controls.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Hosts can be replaced, so hostnames cannot be the durable work identity.

items.prompt: The shared session store is unavailable during a partial outage. What should the application do?
constraints: The store is required for authenticated state.
The system must not silently authenticate users.
The product has a defined degraded experience.

options.text: Expose an explicit unavailable or reauthentication state, fail closed for protected operations, and recover through the store's availability design rather than inventing sessions.
Create a new authenticated session locally without checking the store so users do not see an error.
Use another user's cached session if it is available in the process.
Return successful business responses from stale session data without checking authorization freshness.

feedback.Reason: When authoritative authentication state is unavailable, a service must not fabricate or borrow identity state.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Fail-closed behavior protects authorization, while explicit error and recovery controls make the dependency failure observable.
Details.scenarioApplication: The client can retry or sign in again according to the product contract, and operators see session-store health and impact metrics.
Details.errorCorrection: Local fabricated sessions, cross-user state, and unverified stale authorization are security failures disguised as availability.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Failing closed can reduce availability, so the store and application need redundancy and a tested recovery plan.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Creating a local authenticated session bypasses the identity authority and can grant unauthorized access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Cross-user session reuse is a critical isolation failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Stale authorization cannot safely justify a successful protected operation.

items.prompt: A shared session store serves multiple tenants. Which key design reduces accidental cross-tenant access?
constraints: Tenant identifiers are part of the authorization context.
Session keys must be unambiguous.
The application validates tenant ownership on every access.

options.text: Partition and namespace records with the tenant identity, enforce authorization in the application and store policy where possible, and test cross-tenant access explicitly.
Use only a short user ID because tenant isolation is guaranteed by the cache cluster name.
Let clients choose the tenant prefix in the key without validating the authenticated tenant.
Use one administrator credential for all tenants so the store can read every record consistently.

feedback.Reason: Tenant identity must be part of the state boundary and authorization check, not an assumption about shared infrastructure.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Namespacing and authorization make the tenant scope explicit in reads and writes and provide a testable isolation invariant.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service derives the tenant from authenticated context, constructs the key, and rejects a request whose tenant does not own the record.
Details.errorCorrection: Cluster-level separation alone does not prevent application key mistakes, client-selected scope is untrusted, and administrator credentials violate least privilege.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Partitioning may affect hot keys and operational layout, so scale and isolation should be tested together.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A shared cluster does not make a short user ID globally or tenant-safe.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Client-controlled tenant scope can be manipulated to access another tenant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Shared administrator access removes tenant-level authorization and attribution.

items.prompt: Which review question most reliably identifies hidden state in an otherwise stateless service?
constraints: The service runs multiple instances.
Instances can be replaced at any time.
The review must cover more than session cookies.

options.text: Ask where every session, upload, idempotency key, lock, cache dependency, temporary file, and business state transition survives instance replacement and failure.
Ask only whether the application has a login screen, because login is the only form of state.
Ask whether all instances have the same hostname, because matching hostnames prove state is shared.
Ask whether CPU is below 50 percent, because low utilization proves no instance-local state exists.

feedback.Reason: Hidden local state often appears in files, locks, idempotency, uploads, or caches even when login state is externalized.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A statelessness review follows all stateful assumptions across request, retry, replacement, and failure paths.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team documents the canonical owner and recovery behavior for each state category and tests instance loss.
Details.errorCorrection: Authentication is only one state type, hostnames do not replicate state, and CPU utilization does not reveal state placement.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A broad review takes time but prevents replacement and scale events from becoming surprise data or availability failures.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Services can hide state in many paths beyond authentication.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Host identity is not state replication or shared durability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Resource utilization does not identify where application state is stored.
